newsitem.title: KENYA: Rising food prices force Kenyan inflation up.
newsitem.headline: Rising food prices force Kenyan inflation up.

text.p: Kenya's three-months overall annualised inflation rose to 14.7 percent in February from 9.4 percent in January on rising food prices and the Central Bank of Kenya on Tuesday expected the trend to continue in March.
The central bank posted month-on-month inflation in February at 11.9 percent from 10.9 percent in January.

Central Bureau of Statistics figures showed the price of maize had risen by 38.5 percent per kg in February from June 1996 while the price of maize flour rose 31.3 percent, kales by 73.9 percent and beans by 40.6 percent in the same period.
The bureau said the price of paraffin had risen by 27.7 percent in February compared to May 1996.
Maize, beans and kales are the main food indicators for lower income group Kenyans, estimated by the central bank at around 76 percent of Kenya's total 28 million population.

"As can be observed, the prices of food commodities have been rising since December. With the current drought, we expect the food prices to continue higher," Bureau Director Margaret Chemengich told a news briefing.

Chemengich said the rising prices were because of a drought that is sweeping through most of East Africa. Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi has already declared the drought a national disaster and appealed for international food aid.
Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem said that as food imports started to arrive, food prices were likely to drop in April, and with these, the annualised overall inflation index.

The state-owned National Cereals and Produce Board (NCPB) on Tuesday said it had awarded tenders to three companies for the supply of 100,000 tonnes of maize for drought victims in Kenya and added the maize must be supplied by end-April.

Cheserem's comments were boosted by bureau figures that showed three-months underlying inflation at 3.8 percent in February from 8.6 percent in January. The underlying inflation figure removed food items from the computation basket.
He said government borrowing from the central bank continued within agreed targets and tight management of such borrowing was responsible for a slow-down in underlying inflation.
"Investors should therefore continue to place increased focus on trends of underlying rather than overall inflation when planning for the future," Cheserem told reporters.
"It is expected that overall inflation will fall once the food supply situation improves through the combination of food imports and the coming of long rains," he said.

"The prime objective of the monetary policy is to contain inflation within single digits. It should be acknowledged that monetary policy, if tightly applied to transitory factors such as the drought, would do damage to the economy," he added.
